artworks.title: Statue of Asclepius from Epidaurus
artworks.artist: Roman copy after a Greek original
artworks.description: A monumental marble Asclepius from his sanctuary at Epidaurus, now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens — the bearded healer with staff and serpent, copied from a Classical Greek type.

artworks.title: Asclepius
artworks.description: A Roman marble of the god of medicine in the Galleria Borghese, Rome — draped, calm, and carrying the serpent-staff that later became medicine's emblem.

artworks.title: Statue of Aesculapius
artworks.description: A Roman marble Aesculapius in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore — the healing god as a standing philosopher-physician, staff coiled with a snake.

artworks.title: A Visit to Aesculapius
artworks.description: Poynter's Tate canvas imagines Venus bringing a thorn-wounded foot to Aesculapius — the Classical healer receiving a goddess in a marble grove, snake-staff at his side.

popCulture.title: Rod of Asclepius
popCulture.description: A single serpent coiled on a staff remains medicine's true emblem — Asclepius' rod on ambulances, hospitals and the WHO seal, distinct from Hermes' twin-snake caduceus.

popCulture.title: Ophiuchus
popCulture.description: The serpent-bearer constellation is often read as Asclepius among the stars — the healer who learned from snakes, written across the summer Milky Way.

popCulture.title: Caduceus as a symbol of medicine
popCulture.description: Modern English still muddles Asclepius' rod with Hermes' caduceus — a standing reminder that the god of medicine and the god of merchants got crossed in print.
